title: Speaking for the Gods
description: Prophets versus diviners, and the oldest prophecies on record, from Mari and Nineveh

concepts.title: Mouthpiece or Diviner?
concepts.contentHtml:
Ask most people what a prophet does and they will say "predicts the future". The ancient word meant something else. The English prophet descends from the Greek prophētēs, a cult official who "spoke for" a god, delivering divine messages at a sanctuary where the god had made its presence known.1 Prediction might be part of the message, but the job was to be a mouthpiece.

Ancient peoples had two broad ways of learning what the gods wanted. Diviners used studied techniques to read signs built into the world: casting lots, sleeping in a temple to receive a dream, examining the entrails of a sacrificed animal, or cataloguing strange events. Oracles worked differently: the god spoke in human language through the mouth of an inspired person, often in a state that onlookers saw as ecstatic or frenzied. Prophets belong to the second group. A diviner had to be trained in a technique; a prophet had to be seized.

Scholars work with a definition rather than a single ancient word. Martti Nissinen, whose 2003 sourcebook gathers the ancient Near Eastern evidence, notes that no language in it, whether Akkadian, Egyptian, Hebrew or other West Semitic, has one word for "prophet". A text counts as prophecy when a deity is the speaker, a human is the addressee, and another human carries the message between them.

Prophets also differed from priests. A priest held office in an established institution and kept the received tradition; a prophet's authority rested on charisma, on being accepted by a community as a channel for a god. One popular picture needs correcting straight away. The lonely prophet crying to deaf ears in the desert is, in the words of the Encyclopedia of Religion, a romantic ideal. In reality groups tend to support prophets who voice their interests, and prophets acting entirely alone rarely find an audience.2

concepts.title: Letters to King Zimri-Lim
concepts.contentHtml:
The oldest prophets whose words survive lived at Mari, a city on the Euphrates in what is now eastern Syria. Between 1933 and 1938 French excavators uncovered more than 15,000 clay tablets there. About fifty letters among them report prophecies, almost all from the reign of King Zimri-Lim, who took the throne in 1776 BCE and lost his city to Hammurabi of Babylon in 1761 BCE. The archive survived by accident: when Hammurabi burned the palace, he baked the clay hard.

The prophets' words reach us second-hand, quoted in letters by officials and by royal women such as Queen Shibtu, who passed messages to the king. The two commonest titles were muhhûm, from a verb meaning "to go into a frenzy", and āpilum, "answerer". They spoke for gods such as Dagan and Annunitum, a form of Ishtar, usually about the king's safety, his wars and the upkeep of temples.

Here is the surprise: a prophecy was not simply believed. The palace often checked it by extispicy, reading the entrails of a sacrificed animal. Letter writers sent the prophet's hair and a fringe of their garment along with the message, so that diviners could test the oracle using these tokens of the prophet.1 Prophets formed an established but not the highest-ranking part of the king's system of divination.

Nor were they always right. Several oracles warned Zimri-Lim against peace with the kingdom of Eshnunna, and he made the alliance anyway. Encouraging oracles promised him victory in his war with Hammurabi; the war ended with Mari destroyed.

concepts.title: Ishtar of Arbela Speaks to Esarhaddon
concepts.contentHtml:
A thousand years after Mari, prophecy turns up again in the archives of Assyria. In the royal archive of Nineveh, discovered by Austen Henry Layard in 1848 to 1850, clay tablets recorded oracles to two kings, Esarhaddon (681 to 669 BCE) and Assurbanipal (668 to 627 BCE). Simo Parpola published them in 1997 as volume 9 of the State Archives of Assyria. The whole corpus is small: no more than twenty-nine individual oracles, only seven on their original tablets.

The oracles have a recognisable voice. Again and again a deity, most often Ishtar of Arbela, tells the king not to be afraid. "Fear not, Esarhaddon! I am Bel, I speak to you!" begins one oracle, delivered by a prophet named Bayâ. The prophets impersonated the deity as they spoke, so the "I" of an oracle is the god. Most oracles promise the king well-being and reconciliation with the gods.

Look at who the speakers were. In Assyria the learned scholars, astrologers, haruspices and exorcists who corresponded with the king were all men, and their expertise was literary. The prophets' expertise lay in being possessed by a deity. Of the thirteen prophets whose personal details survive in the oracles, eight are women,1 and in two or three cases, Bayâ among them, the gender is unclear, perhaps because these people lived in an undefined gender role. Their names are small sermons in themselves, such as Ilussa-amur, "I have seen her divinity".

The tablets also show something new. Some oracles were copied from single reports onto larger tablets that gathered several together for long-term keeping. Nissinen sees here the modest beginnings of a process of collecting and reusing prophecy that, in Israel, would grow into whole books.

title: The Prophets of Israel
description: Seers and ecstatic bands, a herdsman who refused the title, and the test of a true prophet

concepts.title: Seers, Bands and Paid Visits
concepts.contentHtml:
The Bible itself admits that its vocabulary changed. An aside in 1 Samuel 9:9 explains that anyone who went to inquire of God used to say "Come, let us go to the seer", "for the one who is now called a prophet was formerly called a seer.1" Early Israel knew several kinds of go-between: cult officers who cast lots and tended sacred objects such as the Ark, seers (ro'eh and hozeh), and ecstatics called navi, the word usually translated "prophet". Over time the navi took over the other roles.

Some early prophets worked in groups. The newly anointed Saul meets "a band of prophets coming down from the high place with harp, tambourine, and lyre", is seized by the spirit and speaks in ecstasy among them, which gave rise to the proverb "Is Saul also among the prophets?" Elisha calls for a musician before he prophesies. Groups called the "disciples of the prophets" ate together, and some members had families.

Prophets also had to make a living. The texts record fees as small as a quarter of a shekel or ten loaves, some cakes and a jar of honey, and as large as forty camels bearing the treasures of Aram.2 Kings consulted them, and so did foreign rulers. When King Josiah sent his officials to inquire of the Lord, they went to a woman, the prophet Huldah, who lived in Jerusalem's Second Quarter (2 Kings 22:14). Later rabbis counted 48 prophets and seven prophetesses whose messages were recorded for future generations.

As at Mari, these prophets often spoke whether anyone asked or not. Elijah, best known for his contest with the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, stops a king's messengers on their way to consult the god Baal-zebub.

concepts.title: "I Am No Prophet": Amos and the Books
concepts.contentHtml:
In the eighth century BCE a new kind of figure appears: the classical or "writing" prophets, whose words were gathered into books. The Encyclopaedia Judaica calls Amos the first of the literary prophets. Their era spans some 300 years, from a few decades before the fall of the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BCE to about a century after the destruction of Jerusalem in 587/6 BCE.

Amos begins with a refusal. Answering Amaziah, he says: "I am no prophet nor a prophet's son, but I am a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore trees, and the Lord took me from following the flock" (Amos 7:14-15). Translators disagree over the tense; the NRSVUE footnote offers "I was no prophet" as an alternative. Is Amos rejecting the title altogether, or saying he was no professional, guild-trained prophet until God called him? Readers still argue. The rabbis even deduced that he was rich: sycamores grow only in the lowland Shephelah and his flocks were in the hills of Tekoa, so he must have owned land in both.

How did spoken oracles become books? Jeremiah 36 tells one story. Jeremiah dictates his words to the scribe Baruch. As the scroll is read aloud, three or four columns at a time are cut off with a penknife and thrown into a brazier, until King Jehoiakim has burned it all. Jeremiah dictates a new scroll, "and many similar words were added to them" (Jeremiah 36:32).1

Scholars see that growth continuing after the prophets died. The books contain supplements and interpolations, such as a late addition to Micah (4:10) that mentions Babylon, and Isaiah from chapter 40 onwards is usually credited to an anonymous later prophet, "Second Isaiah". Nissinen points out that this huge process of collecting, editing and interpreting prophecy is virtually without precedent elsewhere in the ancient Near East.2

concepts.title: True Prophet or False?
concepts.contentHtml:
If two prophets contradict each other in the name of the same God, whom do you believe? Deuteronomy offers a test: "If a prophet speaks in the name of the Lord but the thing does not take place or prove true, it is a word that the Lord has not spoken" (Deuteronomy 18:22). Deuteronomy 13 adds another: a prophet who performs signs and wonders but urges the worship of other gods must still be refused.

Jeremiah 28 shows how hard the first test is to apply. The prophet Hananiah announces in the Lord's name that the yoke of Babylon will be broken and that within two years the exiles and King Jehoiachin will come home. Jeremiah, who had been urging submission to Babylon, says he wishes it were true, but that a prophet who promises peace is known to be sent by God only when his word comes to pass. Then he walks away. Later he returns with a new message: Hananiah will die within the year. The chapter ends: "In that same year, in the seventh month, the prophet Hananiah died.1"

Notice what the Hebrew does not say. It calls both men navi. There is no term for a false prophet in the Hebrew Bible; the label2 pseudoprophētēs was introduced by the Greek translation into some verses of Jeremiah and Zechariah. Most "false" prophets spoke sincerely in the name of Israel's God, and the fulfilment test was useless at the moment a prophecy was spoken, when people had to decide what to do.

The test was awkward for "true" prophets too. Ezekiel predicted that Nebuchadnezzar would destroy Tyre, and later acknowledged that the siege had failed (Ezekiel 26 and 29). Jeremiah's forecast of a shameful end for King Jehoiakim does not match the account in 2 Kings, and the hopes Haggai and Zechariah placed in Zerubbabel came to nothing. The books kept these unfulfilled oracles alongside the fulfilled ones.

title: Sibyls and Sacred Books
description: Rome's Sibylline Books, prophecies written in the Sibyl's name, and sibyls in Christian art

concepts.title: Nine Books, One Price
concepts.contentHtml:
Greece and Rome had inspired women of their own. The most famous, the Pythia at Delphi, answered questions in Apollo's name; her supposed vapours are a story for another topic. The sibyls were different: legendary prophetesses whose verses circulated in writing. Early Greek writers speak of "the sibyl" in the singular, later authors of many. The Roman scholar Varro, quoted by the Christian writer Lactantius, counted ten, including sibyls of Persia, Libya, Delphi, Erythrae, Cumae and Tibur.

Rome's own sibylline story is a lesson in bargaining. As the Greek historian Dionysius of Halicarnassus tells it, a foreign woman offered King Tarquinius nine books of Sibylline oracles. He refused her price, so she burned three and asked the same sum for the six that were left. Mocked again, she burned three more. Uneasy, Tarquinius consulted the augurs, who told him he had rejected a gift from the gods, and he paid the full price for the last three. Ancient writers did not even agree on which king it was. Dionysius tells the story of Tarquinius Superbus, Rome's last king, while Varro's version names Tarquinius Priscus and calls the seller the Sibyl of Cumae, Amalthaea.1

The books became state property of the highest order. Two distinguished citizens guarded them, helped by public slaves. When one guardian, Marcus Atilius, was accused of betraying his trust, Tarquinius had him sewn into a leather bag and thrown into the sea, the punishment for parricide. The keepers later became ten, and after Sulla fifteen, the quindecimviri. The senate ordered the books consulted only in crises: civil strife, disaster in war, or strange prodigies. Dionysius says the Romans guarded no possession, sacred or profane, so carefully.

concepts.title: Fire, a Forgery Test and an Emperor's Bonfire
concepts.contentHtml:
For centuries the books lay underground in the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol, in a stone chest. Then, in 83 BCE, the temple burned, "either purposely, as some think, or by accident", and the oracles burned with it. Rome needed new ones. Three envoys were sent by vote of the senate to Erythrae in Asia Minor to copy verses there,1 and others were gathered from the cities of Italy and from private copies.

How do you rebuild a sacred text from scattered copies without letting forgeries in? The Romans had a test. Genuine Sibylline oracles, written in Greek hexameters, were held to be acrostics: the first letters of the lines spelled out words. Verses that broke the pattern could be exposed as interpolations. It was a check on authenticity built into the poetry itself.

The collecting worked too well. By the time Augustus became chief priest, pontifex maximus, on the death of Lepidus, prophetic writings in Greek and Latin were circulating everywhere, some anonymous, some under obscure names. Suetonius reports that Augustus gathered them up and burned more than two thousand, keeping only the Sibylline books, and even those only after making a selection.2 He placed the survivors in two gilded cases under the pedestal of the statue of Apollo on the Palatine.

Think about what this means for the books' contents. What Rome consulted after 83 BCE was a reconstruction, assembled from other cities' copies, screened by a test of form, then pruned on an emperor's orders. Ancient authority could be rebuilt, and edited, by committee.

concepts.title: The Sibyl Turns Jewish, Then Christian
concepts.contentHtml:
The Sibylline Oracles you can read today are not Rome's books. They are a separate collection of Greek hexameter poems written in the sibyls' names by Jews and Christians. According to the 1912 Catholic Encyclopedia, Hellenistic Jews in Alexandria began composing such verses in the second century BCE to spread Jewish teaching among pagans,1 and Christians later revised the Jewish books and added their own. Part of Book VIII is an acrostic on the Greek word ichthys, "fish", a Christian symbol. Even then the encyclopedia admitted that scholars could not settle exactly which parts were Jewish and which Christian.

The borrowed voice worked. Early Christian writers from Justin to Augustine quoted the sibyls, and Lactantius argued that all ten of Varro's sibyls proclaimed one God. Pagan prophetesses became witnesses for Christianity. That is why a sibyl appears in the opening stanza of the hymn sung at the requiem Mass, the Dies irae: "Dies iræ, dies illa, solvet sæclum in favilla, teste David cum Sibylla", "the day of wrath, that day, will dissolve the world in ashes, as David and the Sibyl bear witness". Its oldest known manuscripts date from the thirteenth century, and it is most often ascribed to the Franciscan Thomas of Celano.

The sibyls reached their grandest stage on the Sistine Chapel ceiling, painted by Michelangelo for Pope Julius II. Twelve prophets and sibyls sit on monumental thrones around the central scenes from Genesis. The Vatican Museums explain that the prophets foresaw Christ for Israel, while the sibyls, "although belonging to the pagan world", are there to extend the wait for redemption from the chosen people to all humanity.

title: The Seal of the Prophets
description: Claims that prophecy ended, and the Báb, Bahá'u'lláh, Ahmadis and Joseph Smith

concepts.title: When Prophecy Ends
concepts.contentHtml:
Several traditions teach that the age of prophecy has closed. In rabbinic Judaism the last prophets were Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, who worked after the return from exile. The Talmud says that when prophecy came to an end, the divine presence departed from Israel1 and a heavenly voice, the bat kol, became a partial substitute (Yoma 9b). The rabbis also held that the prophets introduced no innovations: they only expounded the teaching of Moses.

Islam makes the most explicit claim. Qur'an 33:40 calls Muhammad khātam an-nabiyyīn. Pickthall, Yusuf Ali and Arberry render it "the Seal of the Prophets"; Sahih International and Shakir translate it directly as "last of the prophets".2 For most Muslims the meaning is settled: no prophet comes after Muhammad. Early Muslims also distinguished a nabi, anyone who has a vision or audition of God, from a rasul, a messenger such as Moses, Jesus or Muhammad who founds a community with a sacred book. (The topic Roots of Religions covers Muhammad's own mission.)

Why do such endings matter? Once a prophet's words were written down and declared scripture, the book replaced the living specialist. Interpreters took over from prophets, and the guardians of scripture were often suspicious of anyone claiming visions that did not come through it. The Encyclopedia of Religion observes that since Muhammad no prophet has founded a tradition with the stature of Judaism, Christianity or Islam.

A closed canon does not stop new claimants; it raises the stakes for them. Anyone announcing a new revelation inside a tradition that says revelation has ended must either reinterpret the ending or found something new. The rest of this lesson follows people who did each.

concepts.title: The Gate and the Glory of God
concepts.contentHtml:
On the evening of 22 May 1844, in Shiraz in Iran, a young merchant named Siyyid 'Alí-Muhammad told a visiting scholar, Mulla Husayn, that he was the bearer of a divine revelation. He took the title the Báb, "the Gate". Within weeks seventeen more followers had joined Mulla Husayn; these eighteen became the "Letters of the Living", among them the poet Tahirih, who called for equality between women and men. The Báb said he was preparing the way for a greater figure, "He Whom God shall make manifest".

Clerics denounced his teaching as heresy, and thousands of his followers were killed. In 1850 the Báb was executed in Tabriz. The Bahá'í community's own account of that day, 9 July, is remarkable: a regiment of 750 soldiers fired three volleys,1 and when the smoke cleared the Báb had vanished, his ropes cut, until he was found back in his cell and shot by a second regiment. It is how Bahá'ís remember the day; the execution and the persecution are not in doubt.

One of the Báb's followers was a nobleman born in Tehran in 1817, Mirza Husayn-'Alí, known as Bahá'u'lláh, "the Glory of God". Chained in 1852 in a dungeon called the Black Pit, he later described feeling "as if something flowed from the crown of My head over My breast". Exiled to Baghdad, in April 1863, in a garden he named Ridván, he declared himself the one the Báb had foretold.2 Further exiles took him to Istanbul, Edirne and finally the prison city of 'Akká, where he spent the rest of his life; he died in 1892.

Bahá'ís see the Báb as the founder of a distinct, independent religion rather than a movement within Islam. They speak of a series of "Manifestations of God", including Moses, the Buddha, Jesus and Muhammad, each a human being called to be a mouthpiece for God for a new age. On this view revelation is progressive rather than closed.

concepts.title: Qadian, Lahore and a Hat in Pennsylvania
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1889, in the Punjab, Mirza Ghulam Ahmad began to take disciples. Two years later he announced that he was both the messiah and the mahdi, and he went on to claim prophethood. Muslim scholars issued rulings condemning him for denying the finality of Muhammad's prophethood. His followers drew a distinction: Muhammad was the last law-bearing prophet, but non-legislative prophets could still come, and they read "seal of the prophets" as "the greatest of the prophets". In 1914 the movement split. The Qadian branch kept the line of caliphs and the belief in his prophethood; the Lahore branch regards him as a reformer, not a prophet.

The dispute became law. Pakistan's Constitution (Second Amendment) Act of 1974 declared that anyone who does not accept the "absolute and unqualified finality" of Muhammad's prophethood, or who recognises a later claimant as a prophet or religious reformer, "is not a Muslim for the purposes of the Constitution or law1". It named both Ahmadi groups. Ordinance XX of 1984 forbade Ahmadis to call themselves Muslims, and the community's head moved to London. Ahmadis describe themselves as Muslims; most Muslims say they are not; as Britain's Religion Media Centre notes, there is no neutral way to word the question.

Outside Islam, too, new prophets kept coming. In the 1820s the young Joseph Smith, like others in his day, used a seer stone to search for lost objects and buried treasure. According to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints' own account, he later often translated the Book of Mormon by placing the stone in a hat and pressing his face into it to block out the light, then reading aloud the English words that appeared to his scribes.2

title: Prophets Against Empire
description: A Shawnee visionary, a West African evangelist, a Zulu hymn-maker and a Congolese prisoner

concepts.title: The Open Door
concepts.contentHtml:
Prophets have often appeared when a way of life was collapsing. The Seneca prophet Handsome Lake and the Paiute prophet Wovoka belong to this story and are covered in the topic Cargo Cults and Colonial Prophets. This lesson follows four others.

Lalawethika, a Shawnee born probably in 1775, was the family failure: named "rattle" or "noisemaker", blind in one eye after an accident, an alcoholic and a poor hunter. In the spring of 1805 he fell into a trance in which, he said, he died and was shown paradise and a hell where drunkards burned. He gave up alcohol, took the name Tenskwatawa, "the open door", and preached that the Master of Life had made the Indians, British, French and Spaniards, but that the Americans were children of the Great Serpent. His followers were to renounce alcohol and much of American culture.

The movement had a dark side: in 1806 he helped Delaware villagers hunt supposed witches, and four were burned at the stake. That year Governor William Henry Harrison tried to discredit him, urging the Delawares to ask the prophet to "cause the sun to stand still". On 16 June 1806 Tenskwatawa successfully predicted a near-total eclipse of the sun, and his influence soared.1 In 1808 he founded Prophetstown at the mouth of the Tippecanoe River. On 7 November 1811, with his brother Tecumseh away, about 700 warriors attacked Harrison's army while Tenskwatawa prayed in the village. The defeat ended his religious leadership.

Here is the myth to bust. White writers long assumed that Tecumseh led the movement from the start and cast his brother as a charlatan. His biographer R. David Edmunds argues the reverse: the prophet's teachings drew the tribes together, and the movement stayed religious until 1810, when Tecumseh began turning it into a military confederacy.2

concepts.title: White Robes and a Holy Mountain
concepts.contentHtml:
William Wade Harris, a Grebo from near Cape Palmas in Liberia, had been a teacher, a catechist and a government interpreter. While in prison during the Grebo rising of 1910, he received, he said, a call from the angel Gabriel to become a prophet. Released around 1912, he put on a white robe and turban and carried a staff in the shape of a cross. In 1913 he walked into the Ivory Coast, preaching against idol worship and healing the sick, and over 100,000 people there converted.1 The French, at first sympathetic, expelled him in 1915 and destroyed his churches. Catholic and Protestant missions competed for his converts, but churches that recognise Harris as their founder still thrive in the Ivory Coast and Ghana.

In South Africa, Isaiah Shembe (about 1870 to 1935) founded the amaNazaretha Baptist Church in 1911, keeping Saturday rather than Sunday as the holy day. In 1912 a revelation sent him up the mountain Inhlangakazi, inland from Durban, for twelve days of temptation. Angels, he said, brought him bread and wine, and he came down with power to heal and drive out demons. An annual pilgrimage to the mountain became a centre of church life.

Shembe's surprise is literary. He remained illiterate until he was about forty, then learned to write so that he could record the hymns, words and melodies together, that came to him in his sleep.2 His Zulu hymnbook, sung alongside dances in traditional Zulu dress, became the heart of the church and is one of the main sources for his faith today. Shembe called himself "the Servant", sent to the Zulu as Moses and Jesus had been sent to the Jews, while affirming Christ's place on the throne of heaven. His son Johannes Galilee succeeded him.

concepts.title: Six Months of Preaching, Thirty Years in Prison
concepts.contentHtml:
Simon Kimbangu, born around 1890 at Nkamba in the Lower Congo, was baptised by the Baptist Missionary Society in 1915. He later said that God's call came during the flu epidemic of 1918 and that he fled to Léopoldville (now Kinshasa) to escape it. On 18 March 1921, back at Nkamba, he had a vision commanding him to preach and heal. Crowds came; workers left the plantations and hospital beds emptied. People called him ngunza, prophet, and Nkamba became the "New Jerusalem". He preached the destruction of fetishes, an end to polygamy and the worship of one God, whom he identified with Nzambi, the Kongo supreme being.

Pressed by Catholic missions and plantation owners, the Belgian authorities saw a threat. Kimbangu gave himself up in September 1921, and a court-martial condemned him to death for disturbing the security of the state. King Albert commuted the sentence to life imprisonment with 120 lashes, and Kimbangu died in prison in Elisabethville (now Lubumbashi) on 12 October 1951, thirty years after a ministry that had lasted barely six months.

Prison made him a martyr-figure, and his followers built an underground church. His son Joseph Diangienda reunited them; on 24 December 1959 the Belgian ban was lifted, and in 1969 the Church of Jesus Christ on Earth by the Prophet Simon Kimbangu became the first independent African church to attain full membership in the World Council of Churches.1

How do historians know any of this? Much comes from colonial and missionary archives, set beside oral histories and the church's own accounts, including a history by Kimbangu's son. Reference works even differ over whether his preaching began in March or April 1921. And defining who Kimbangu was has always been theologically difficult, for missionaries, Western scholars and Kimbanguist theologians alike.

title: The Prophecy Trade
description: Nostradamus, Mother Shipton's forged verses, Joanna Southcott's box and why vague prophecy works

concepts.title: Nostradamus and the Hister Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
Michel de Nostredame was born in 1503 at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence into a family of Catholic converts from Judaism. He studied medicine at Montpellier, made his name fighting plague, and settled around 1547 in Salon-de-Provence, where his income came more and more from horoscopes and almanacs. In 1555 a Lyon press issued his Prophéties, some 350 verses in obscure French, arranged in groups of a hundred called "centuries". The full corpus eventually reached 942 four-line quatrains.

The verses follow no chronological order, contain few dates, and announce wars, plots and disasters in vivid but slippery language. That is their strength. The historian Stéphane Gerson, in a 2012 study, shows that readers rarely read the book straight through. They jumped between quatrains, seizing on any that seemed to fit current events. Quatrain 1.35 was read as foretelling Henri II's death in a jousting accident in 1559, and it made Nostradamus famous. Two readers, unaware of each other, applied quatrain 1.53 to John Law's Mississippi bubble of 1720. Others found Napoleon, and in the 1960s the Kennedys.

The most famous case is the word "Hister" in quatrain 2.24, taken in the twentieth century as a prediction of Hitler. Gerson argues persuasively that it is an archaic name for the Danube.1 A near-match of letters did the rest.

Nostradamus was not even the only author of "Nostradamus". An industry grew up around him, issuing new editions, sometimes with new quatrains written for their own times and falsely attributed to him, along with guides explaining what the old ones really meant. Interest in him rises in times of war and crisis and falls in times of peace.

concepts.title: Mother Shipton's Forged Verses
concepts.contentHtml:
England's favourite prophetess may never have existed. Mother Shipton first appears in print in a pamphlet of 1641, which claimed she had foretold the death of Cardinal Wolsey. Later chapbooks by Richard Head and others added a birth from a union between her mother and the Devil and, eventually, a baptismal name, Ursula Sonthiel, and a birth date in 1488. There is no evidence that she made the prophecies, or even that she was a real person.

Her most famous verses are a Victorian fake. In 1862 the bookseller Charles Hindley published a chapbook he said was reprinted from Head's, with rhymes in which Shipton seemed to foresee steamships and the telegraph and, in a final couplet, the end of the world in 1881. In 1873 Hindley confessed in the journal Notes and Queries that he had made the verses up. It made no difference. In 1881 the couplet caused real panic in country districts; people left their houses to spend the night in the fields or praying in churches and chapels. As one encyclopedia drily notes, ordinary country people did not read learned antiquarian journals.1

Why do forged or vague prophecies stick? Psychologists describe the Barnum effect: people judge vague, general statements to be highly accurate descriptions of themselves, as with horoscopes and personality tests.2 Bertram Forer's 1949 paper, subtitled "a classroom demonstration of gullibility", is the classic demonstration. Add retrofitting (matching a verse to an event after it happens), selective memory (the misses are forgotten) and sheer numbers of verses, and some will always seem to come true. Hindley had an extra advantage: he wrote his "predictions" after steamships and the telegraph already existed.

concepts.title: Joanna Southcott's Box
concepts.contentHtml:
Joanna Southcott, born in 1750 to a Devon farming family, was a domestic servant in Exeter when, in the 1790s, she began to hear a voice. It foretold events great and small, and she wrote its messages at speed, often in simple verse. When clergymen ignored her demands to examine her writings, she spent her savings publishing The Strange Effects of Faith in 1801. She issued thousands of paper "seals" to believers and gathered more than eight thousand disciples. Many of her prophecies were sealed up in a box.

In 1814, aged 64, she announced that she would give birth to Shiloh, a divine child. She showed signs of pregnancy, which a leading surgeon and some twenty other practitioners confirmed, and gifts poured in, including a satinwood cradle. No child came. In her will she said she had been deceived by the Devil, and she died on 27 December 1814. Doctors found no organic disease beyond dropsy, which may have heightened a false pregnancy.

The box outlived her. Her instructions, as later summarised, were that it be opened after a hundred years in the presence of 24 bishops. Believers kept up the pressure, above all a community in Bedford that became the Panacea Society, and for decades newspaper notices warned that crime and disaster would increase until the bishops opened the box. In 1927 the psychical researcher Harry Price said he had been sent the box and opened it before an audience at Church House, Westminster, on 11 July. Only one bishop came, the bishop of Grantham.1 Inside were a horse pistol, a lottery ticket for 1796, a woman's nightcap, a dice cup, coins and some old books. Southcott's followers replied that this was not the true box.

title: Hearing the Voice
description: Charisma after the prophet dies, Jaynes's bicameral mind, and what voice-hearing research shows

concepts.title: When the Prophet Dies
concepts.contentHtml:
The topic Classical Social Theory introduces Max Weber's three kinds of authority. Prophets are a model case of the first, charisma: authority that rests on followers' belief that a person has extraordinary, even divine, gifts. The sociologist Edward Shils, summarising Weber, names the problem: the inevitability of death and the need for succession force charisma to spread out from a few persons into offices, lineages, governing bodies and rules.1 Weber called this the routinisation of charisma. The prophets in this topic show the main ways it can go.

  • A written will. Bahá'u'lláh's will named his son 'Abdu'l-Bahá as successor. Bahá'ís regard this as the first time a founder of a world religion named a successor in a written text,2 and they credit this "Covenant" with keeping the community united.
  • A split. After the death of Ghulam Ahmad's first successor, the Ahmadiyya divided in 1914 over the founder's status, and the two branches remain separate.
  • A family line. Kimbangu's son Joseph Diangienda reunited his scattered followers, and Shembe's son Johannes Galilee succeeded him.
  • Rival heirs. Joanna Southcott's death produced a chain of claimants: George Turner, who announced Shiloh's birth for dates in 1820 and 1821; John Wroe, whose Christian Israelite church continues in Australia; James Jezreel; and the Panacea Society in Bedford.

Weber's scheme also explains the endings in lesson 4. A tradition that declares prophecy finished has completed its routinisation: authority now belongs to scripture and to those trained to interpret it. As Shils puts it, the custodians of routine order keep up barriers against charismatic newcomers, which is one reason new prophets so often meet resistance.

concepts.title: Jaynes and the Bicameral Mind
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1976 the Princeton psychologist Julian Jaynes published The Origin of Consciousness in the Breakdown of the Bicameral Mind, one of the boldest theories ever proposed about prophets. Jaynes argued that consciousness as we know it, an inner space where we narrate and decide, is learned through language and is only about 3,000 years old. Before it, he proposed, people did not deliberate: when a decision was needed, a voice told them what to do, and they obeyed. "To me this is the origin of gods," he said in a 1983 lecture; he regarded the voices as auditory hallucinations, perhaps produced as the right hemisphere of the brain "talked" to the left.

On this view, prophets were survivors. Comparing the Book of Amos, which he dated to about 800 BCE, with Ecclesiastes, from about 200 BCE, Jaynes suggested that "such prophets as Amos were those left-over bicameral or semi-bicameral persons in the conscious era1", prized because they could still relay the voice of Yahweh with convincing authenticity. Divination, oracles and prophets, in his scheme, were what remained as the voices fell silent.

The theory has devoted defenders; the Julian Jaynes Society keeps a long table of evidence, and to its credit lists the standard objections beside it. A text without words for inner thought may reflect literary style rather than a missing mind,2 and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy notes that Neolithic burials already suggest reflective thought. This topic adds two problems. Prophetic books were collected, expanded and edited, so their style tells you about scribes as much as prophets. And Jaynes reads Amos 7:14 as a shepherd boy who "does not even know what the word means", where the Encyclopaedia Judaica reads Amos as setting himself apart from guild prophets.

concepts.title: What Voice-Hearing Research Shows
concepts.contentHtml:
Hearing a voice that no one else hears is more common than many people assume. A 2017 systematic review by Baumeister and colleagues cites a meta-analysis estimating a median prevalence of 6% for hallucinatory experiences in the general population. Jaynes, citing a 1983 study, had put auditory hallucinations at about half the population at some time; figures depend heavily on how a hallucination is defined and asked about. The review examined 36 studies comparing "healthy voice-hearers", who need no psychiatric care, with patients.

Its findings are striking. How the voices sound, their loudness and whether they seem inside or outside the head, is similar in both groups. What differs is everything around the voice: healthy voice-hearers hear voices less often, with less negative content and more sense of control, and they suffer less distress. They also more often make sense of the experience through spiritual or religious frameworks. In one study, religious healthy voice-hearers more often heard "God" and rarely "the Devil", while patients more often heard "the Devil" and rarely "God".1

The Stanford anthropologist Tanya Luhrmann, author of When God Talks Back (2012), asks why some people hear gods and others do not. In a 2021 study with colleagues, covering more than 2,000 participants in the United States, Ghana, Thailand, China and Vanuatu, two factors predicted vivid experiences of gods and spirits.2 One is cultural: a "porous" model of the mind, in which thoughts and spirits can pass between mind and world. The other is personal: absorption, the capacity to become engrossed in sensory or imagined experience, such as losing yourself in music.

What does this research show, and what not? It shows that hearing a voice is not by itself a sign of illness, and that culture and inner habits shape who hears what. It cannot tell you whether any voice comes from a god. That question lies beyond what psychology or history can settle, and this topic has left it open throughout.
